name: Experimental Psychology
description: An introduction to the scientific methods, research designs, statistical tools, and ethical standards used to conduct and evaluate psychological research.

modules.title: Science & the Scientific Method
modules.objectives: Describe the goals and characteristics of science, explain the steps of the scientific method, and distinguish science from pseudoscience.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — scientific reasoning, theories, hypotheses, and replication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Science & the Scientific Method; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — compare descriptive, correlational, and experimental approaches.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A fictional article claims that students who keep plants on their desks earn higher grades. It reports one classroom observation, no comparison group, and no measure of prior achievement. Task: Write a research-logic brief that separates observation from explanation, proposes two falsifiable hypotheses, lists the evidence each predicts, and explains why one favorable example cannot confirm the claim. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: claim/evidence distinction 25%; hypotheses and predictions 30%; falsifiability reasoning 30%; clarity 15%.

modules.title: Research Ethics
modules.objectives: Explain the key principles of ethical research (informed consent, deception, debriefing, confidentiality), and evaluate landmark ethical violations in psychology.
modules.readingNote: U.S. HHS — Belmont Report primary source on respect, beneficence, and justice.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Research Ethics; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: U.S. HHS — informed-consent guidance for evaluating a fictional protocol.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A fictional study asks 14–16-year-olds to complete an unspecified stress task. Parents receive only a broad permission form; students are told they cannot stop once the timer begins; names appear in the working dataset; and the comparison group is recruited only from advanced classes. The protocol does not state the task intensity, data-access rules, de-identification timing, compensation, debriefing, or support plan. Task: Prepare an IRB-style review applying respect, beneficence, and justice. Separate established problems from possible risks and missing information; classify each supplied feature as an established ethical problem, a possible risk, or a fact that needs more information, and state at least two questions that must be answered; rate the risk only as far as the evidence permits; specify assent/consent, withdrawal, confidentiality, equitable-recruitment, and debriefing safeguards; and recommend approve, revise, or reject. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied facts, and reasoning that connects the facts to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: Belmont application 30%; problem/risk/evidence classification 30%; safeguards 25%; decision clarity 15%.

modules.title: Observational Methods
modules.objectives: Distinguish between naturalistic and structured observation, describe participant vs. non-participant observation, and evaluate the strengths and limitations of observational research.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax — naturalistic observation, case studies, surveys, and archival research.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Observational Methods; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Simply Psychology — structured overview of observation, coding, reactivity, and reliability.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Two observers code eight 20-second fictional classroom intervals as On-task or Off-task. Observer A: O,O,F,O,F,O,O,F. Observer B: O,F,F,O,F,O,O,O. A note says students saw the observers enter after interval 4. Task: Calculate raw percent agreement, identify the disagreement intervals, explain one limitation of percent agreement, and propose a revised coding protocol addressing operational definition, observer training, and reactivity. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: calculation 25%; discrepancy analysis 20%; reliability limitation 20%; redesign 35%.

modules.title: Survey & Self-Report Methods
modules.objectives: Explain the principles of effective survey design, identify common response biases, and compare open-ended and closed-ended question formats.
modules.readingNote: Pew Research Center — survey wording, order, and response-option design.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Survey & Self-Report Methods; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e §2.2 — survey research, sampling, response quality, and limits of self-report.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A six-item fictional survey contains: (1) 'Responsible students always finish homework before gaming, right?' [Yes/No]; (2) 'How safe and welcoming is your school?' [Excellent/Good/Poor]; (3) 'How many hours of homework do you do?' [0–1, 2–3, 4–5, 6+; no timeframe]; (4) 'Have you bullied another student this month?' [Yes/No; student name required]; (5) 'Overall, how satisfied are you with school?' [Very satisfied to Very dissatisfied], placed immediately after Item 4; and (6) 'Don't you agree the new schedule is much better?' [Strongly agree/Agree/Neutral]. Task: Diagnose at least six wording, response-option, order, or privacy problems. Rewrite all six items using neutral wording, a clear timeframe where needed, balanced and exhaustive options, and a privacy-sensitive choice; then justify two design choices. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied items, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each revision. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: diagnosis 30%; revised items 35%; design justification 25%; clarity 10%.

modules.title: Correlational Research
modules.objectives: Explain what a correlation coefficient measures, interpret scatter plots, and explain why correlation does not imply causation. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax — correlation, interpretation, and limits on causal claims.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Correlational Research; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Spurious Correlations — practice spotting why association alone does not establish causation.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Fictional weekly data for eight students give study hours [2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9] and quiz scores [58,62,61,69,72,74,81,83]. The dataset does not include prior achievement, tutoring, or sleep. Task: Create a scatterplot, describe direction/form/strength without claiming causation, calculate or estimate the correlation using a spreadsheet, identify two plausible third variables, and write a bounded conclusion. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: graph/calculation 30%; correlation interpretation 25%; third-variable reasoning 25%; bounded conclusion 20%.

modules.title: Experimental Design
modules.objectives: Identify the components of a true experiment, distinguish between between-subjects and within-subjects designs, and explain the importance of control groups.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e §2.3 — experiments, variables, control groups, random assignment, and causal inference.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Experimental Design; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e §2.3 — apply experimental-design and validity checks to the fictional protocol.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A fictional school tests whether 10 minutes of retrieval practice improves vocabulary. Forty students are available; classes meet at different times; one teacher created both tests; and students may discuss the activity between sessions. Task: Design a paper-only randomized experiment specifying IV, DV, operational definitions, comparison condition, assignment method, standardization, blinding where feasible, ethics, and a plan for contamination and attrition. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: design completeness 30%; control/randomization 30%; validity/ethics 25%; clarity 15%.

modules.title: Variables & Control
modules.objectives: Operationally define independent, dependent, and confounding variables, explain experimental control techniques, and recognize sources of bias. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e §2.3 — operational definitions, confounds, control, reliability, and validity.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Variables & Control; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — evaluate measurement quality and alternative explanations.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A fictional experiment compares quiet and music conditions, but the quiet group tests at 8 a.m. with paper instructions while the music group tests at 2 p.m. on tablets. The outcome is 'focus' judged informally by the teacher. Task: Identify every confound and measurement problem, propose an operational definition of focus, redesign the study so only the intended IV differs, and distinguish reliability from construct validity. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: confound inventory 30%; operational definition 25%; controlled redesign 30%; reliability/validity distinction 15%.

modules.title: Sampling Methods
modules.objectives: Compare probability and non-probability sampling techniques, explain sampling error, and evaluate how sample characteristics affect generalizability. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introductory Statistics §1.2 — probability samples, stratification, sampling bias, and variation.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Sampling Methods; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Introductory Statistics — populations, samples, bias, and variation.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Fictional North Valley High enrolls 480 Grade 9, 420 Grade 10, 360 Grade 11, and 240 Grade 12 students. A 150-student sample is needed. The only easy list contains after-school club members. Task: Calculate a proportionate stratified allocation by grade, explain how to randomly select within strata, compare the plan with convenience and simple random sampling, and predict coverage/nonresponse risks. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: allocation accuracy 30%; sampling procedure 25%; method comparison 25%; bias analysis 20%.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of psychological science?
quizQuestions.answer: Entertainment
quizQuestions.explanation: The four goals of psychology are description, explanation, prediction, and control/application — not entertainment.

quizQuestions.question: A testable prediction derived from a theory is called a:
quizQuestions.answer: Hypothesis
quizQuestions.explanation: A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about the relationship between variables derived from theory.

quizQuestions.question: A scientific claim is falsifiable when:
options: No result could count against it
Some possible observation could show it is wrong
quizQuestions.answer: Some possible observation could show it is wrong
quizQuestions.explanation: Falsifiability requires the claim to rule out at least one possible observable outcome.

quizQuestions.question: Informed consent requires that participants:
options: Are fully deceived about the study's purpose
Cannot withdraw from a study once begun
Are told enough about the study to make a voluntary decision to participate
quizQuestions.answer: Are told enough about the study to make a voluntary decision to participate
quizQuestions.explanation: Informed consent is an ethical requirement that participants receive sufficient information about the study to decide whether to participate voluntarily.

quizQuestions.question: Debriefing in research involves:
options: Obtaining consent before the study begins
Explaining the true purpose of the study after it ends
quizQuestions.answer: Explaining the true purpose of the study after it ends
quizQuestions.explanation: Debriefing informs participants about any deception used and the full purpose of the study, allowing them to make sense of their experience.

quizQuestions.question: The Belmont Report established which three core principles of research ethics?
quizQuestions.answer: Respect, justice, beneficence
quizQuestions.explanation: The Belmont Report (1979) identified three principles: respect for persons (autonomy), beneficence (do good/avoid harm), and justice (fair distribution of benefits and risks).

quizQuestions.question: When research deception is proposed, an ethics review should first ask whether:
options: It is necessary, minimizes risk, and will be followed by meaningful debriefing
Participants can never learn the true purpose
It will make the results more surprising
quizQuestions.answer: It is necessary, minimizes risk, and will be followed by meaningful debriefing
quizQuestions.explanation: Deception requires strong justification, minimized risk, protection of autonomy, and timely debriefing.

quizQuestions.question: Naturalistic observation requires researchers to:
options: Observe behavior without interfering in natural settings
quizQuestions.answer: Observe behavior without interfering in natural settings
quizQuestions.explanation: Naturalistic observation involves watching and recording behavior as it occurs naturally, without intervention.

quizQuestions.question: The observer effect (Hawthorne effect) refers to:
options: The difficulty of remaining objective while observing
Behavior changing because participants know they are being observed
quizQuestions.answer: Behavior changing because participants know they are being observed
quizQuestions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect occurs when awareness of being observed changes participants' behavior, threatening the naturalness of the observation.

quizQuestions.question: Inter-rater reliability in observational research refers to:
options: Whether the same observer gives consistent ratings over time
The consistency of the observation coding scheme across studies
Whether the measure captures what it intends to measure
Agreement between two or more independent observers
quizQuestions.answer: Agreement between two or more independent observers
quizQuestions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability measures the degree of agreement between independent observers using the same coding system.

quizQuestions.question: A Likert scale typically measures:
options: Degree of agreement or disagreement on a numbered scale
quizQuestions.answer: Degree of agreement or disagreement on a numbered scale
quizQuestions.explanation: Likert scales ask respondents to rate their agreement from strongly disagree to strongly agree, providing ordered response options.

quizQuestions.question: Social desirability bias in surveys refers to respondents:
options: Giving answers they believe are socially acceptable rather than truthful
quizQuestions.answer: Giving answers they believe are socially acceptable rather than truthful
quizQuestions.explanation: Social desirability bias occurs when respondents give answers that make them look good rather than answering honestly.

quizQuestions.question: A leading question in survey research is problematic because it:
options: Suggests the desired answer within the question
quizQuestions.answer: Suggests the desired answer within the question
quizQuestions.explanation: Leading questions bias responses by hinting at a desired or expected answer, compromising the validity of survey data.

quizQuestions.question: Open-ended survey questions are advantageous because they:
options: Capture a range of unexpected responses in participants' own words
quizQuestions.answer: Capture a range of unexpected responses in participants' own words
quizQuestions.explanation: Open-ended questions allow respondents to answer freely, potentially revealing unexpected themes not anticipated by the researcher.

quizQuestions.question: A correlation coefficient of +0.90 indicates:
quizQuestions.answer: A strong positive relationship
quizQuestions.explanation: Correlation coefficients close to +1.0 indicate a strong positive (direct) relationship between two variables.

quizQuestions.question: A third variable problem in correlational research means:
options: A third variable may account for the observed relationship between both measured variables
Three variables must always be measured simultaneously
quizQuestions.answer: A third variable may account for the observed relationship between both measured variables
quizQuestions.explanation: An unmeasured factor can influence both variables or otherwise explain their association; correlation alone does not show that either measured variable causes the other.

quizQuestions.question: In a simple two-variable analysis, a correlation of r = .90 has an r-squared of approximately:
quizQuestions.explanation: Squaring .90 gives .81, indicating about 81% shared variance in this simplified bivariate model; it still does not establish causation.

quizQuestions.question: Which conclusion is justified by a strong correlation between sleep and grades?
options: The variables are associated, but causal direction and third variables remain unresolved
More sleep definitely causes every grade increase
quizQuestions.answer: The variables are associated, but causal direction and third variables remain unresolved
quizQuestions.explanation: Strength of association does not eliminate reverse causation, confounding, or measurement problems.

quizQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of random assignment in an experiment?
options: To select a representative population sample
To guarantee identical groups in every realized sample
To ensure every participant receives every condition
To make treatment groups comparable on average by allocating participant differences by chance
quizQuestions.answer: To make treatment groups comparable on average by allocating participant differences by chance
quizQuestions.explanation: Random assignment reduces systematic allocation bias and balances characteristics in expectation, but chance imbalance can remain, especially in small samples.

quizQuestions.question: In a within-subjects (repeated measures) design, each participant:
options: Is assigned to only one condition
Is matched with a participant in another condition
Is compared only to the control group
Experiences all conditions of the experiment
quizQuestions.answer: Experiences all conditions of the experiment
quizQuestions.explanation: In a within-subjects design, the same participants are tested in all conditions, reducing individual-difference confounds.

quizQuestions.question: A control group in an experiment serves as:
options: A replication of the experimental group
The group receiving the highest dose of the treatment
A baseline for comparison with the experimental group
The group assigned randomly to conditions
quizQuestions.answer: A baseline for comparison with the experimental group
quizQuestions.explanation: A control or comparison group provides a baseline. Depending on the question, it may receive no treatment, a placebo, usual practice, or an active comparison condition.

quizQuestions.question: In a repeated-measures experiment, counterbalancing is used mainly to reduce:
quizQuestions.answer: Order and carryover effects
quizQuestions.explanation: Varying condition order helps separate the treatment effect from practice, fatigue, or carryover effects.

quizQuestions.question: An operational definition specifies:
options: The ethical justification for the study
The statistical analysis to be used
How a variable will be measured or manipulated in a specific study
The theoretical meaning of a construct
quizQuestions.answer: How a variable will be measured or manipulated in a specific study
quizQuestions.explanation: Operational definitions translate abstract constructs into concrete, measurable procedures used in a specific study.

quizQuestions.question: Experimenter bias occurs when:
options: The researcher's expectations influence the outcome of the study
quizQuestions.answer: The researcher's expectations influence the outcome of the study
quizQuestions.explanation: Experimenter bias is the unintentional influence of a researcher's expectations on how they collect, interpret, or report data.

quizQuestions.question: A confounding variable is one that:
options: Is held constant across every condition
Varies with the intended IV and offers an alternative explanation for the DV
quizQuestions.answer: Varies with the intended IV and offers an alternative explanation for the DV
quizQuestions.explanation: A confound changes systematically with condition, so the observed effect cannot be attributed uniquely to the intended IV.

quizQuestions.question: Which definition best describes a simple random sample of a fixed size?
options: The researcher selects equal numbers from every subgroup
Every possible sample of that size has an equal chance of selection
Each selected person must be chosen independently even when sampling without replacement
The easiest available participants are invited
quizQuestions.answer: Every possible sample of that size has an equal chance of selection
quizQuestions.explanation: A simple random sample gives each possible sample of the specified size an equal selection probability; selection events need not be independent when sampling without replacement.

quizQuestions.question: In proportionate stratified random sampling, the researcher divides the population into subgroups and then:
options: Randomly samples from each subgroup in proportion to its population size
Uses the same number from each subgroup regardless of size
Chooses only volunteers within each subgroup
Selects every member of one subgroup
quizQuestions.answer: Randomly samples from each subgroup in proportion to its population size
quizQuestions.explanation: Proportionate allocation preserves subgroup shares while random selection occurs within each stratum; other stratified designs may use disproportionate allocation.

quizQuestions.question: A convenience sample is a limitation because it:
options: Cannot be used in correlational research
Is unlikely to be representative of the population
Is too large for statistical analysis
quizQuestions.answer: Is unlikely to be representative of the population
quizQuestions.explanation: Convenience samples consist of participants who are easily available, which can introduce systematic bias and limit generalizability.

quizQuestions.question: A school sampling frame contains only after-school club members. What is the main threat to generalizability?
options: Random assignment failure within an experiment
Perfect representation because clubs include volunteers
Coverage bias because students outside clubs have no chance of selection
quizQuestions.answer: Coverage bias because students outside clubs have no chance of selection
quizQuestions.explanation: A frame limited to club members systematically excludes part of the target population, even if selection from the club list is random.

questions.question: A claim says an invisible force always changes whenever a test could disconfirm it. Which feature of science is the claim missing?
questions.answer: Falsifiability
questions.explanation: A scientific claim must rule out at least one observable outcome; changing the claim after every result prevents a possible disconfirmation.

questions.question: Debriefing is ethically required after research involving:
questions.answer: Deception or potentially distressing procedures
questions.explanation: Debriefing is especially critical when deception or distress was involved, ensuring participants fully understand what occurred and why.

questions.question: Students begin sitting unusually still immediately after observers enter the room. Which threat to the observation is most plausible?
questions.answer: Reactivity to being observed
questions.explanation: Behavior that changes because observation becomes noticeable threatens the naturalness of the record.

questions.question: Students complete a named survey for their teacher asking whether they cheated. Which response problem should the researcher anticipate most directly?
questions.answer: Social desirability bias
questions.explanation: Respondents may underreport stigmatized conduct when answers are identifiable and linked to an authority figure.

questions.question: A scatter plot shows a tight cluster of points on a line sloping upward — this indicates:
questions.answer: A strong positive correlation
questions.explanation: A tight upward-sloping scatter indicates a strong positive relationship between the two variables.

questions.question: Forty students are assigned to two conditions by a concealed random-number generator. Which conclusion about the groups is justified before treatment?
options: Any later difference must be caused by treatment even if procedures differ
The sample is automatically representative of all students
The groups are guaranteed identical on every characteristic
Assignment reduces systematic allocation bias and balances traits in expectation, but chance imbalance may remain
questions.answer: Assignment reduces systematic allocation bias and balances traits in expectation, but chance imbalance may remain
questions.explanation: Random assignment supports causal inference by preventing systematic allocation, but it does not guarantee exact balance or control later procedural confounds.

questions.question: A study defines “focus” as the number of correctly completed target items in a 10-minute task. This statement is the study’s:
questions.answer: Operational definition of focus
questions.explanation: The statement translates an abstract construct into a specified, measurable procedure.

questions.question: A school wants its sample to preserve grade-level proportions while using random selection within each grade. Which method fits this goal?
questions.answer: Proportionate stratified random sampling
questions.explanation: The population is divided into grade strata, allocated in proportion to enrollment, and sampled randomly within each grade.

questions.question: Construct validity refers to whether a test:
options: Truly measures the psychological construct it intends to measure
questions.answer: Truly measures the psychological construct it intends to measure
questions.explanation: Construct validity evaluates whether the measurement instrument accurately taps the theoretical construct it is designed to assess.

questions.question: A school-satisfaction item appears immediately after a sensitive bullying question. Which survey concern is most relevant?
options: Observers may disagree on behavior codes
Question-order context may influence the satisfaction response
questions.answer: Question-order context may influence the satisfaction response
questions.explanation: Earlier questions can prime emotions or topics that change how respondents interpret and answer a later item.

questions.question: In a double-blind experiment, who does NOT know which participants received the treatment?
questions.answer: Both participants and the experimenter
questions.explanation: In a double-blind design, both participants and the people administering the study are unaware of condition assignment, controlling for multiple sources of bias.

questions.question: Two observers agree on 6 of 8 independently coded intervals. What is the raw percent agreement?
questions.explanation: Raw percent agreement is 6 ÷ 8 × 100 = 75%; a fuller reliability analysis may also account for chance agreement.

questions.question: The directionality problem in correlational research means:
options: Three variables must always be measured
We cannot determine which variable caused the other
questions.answer: We cannot determine which variable caused the other
questions.explanation: Correlational data show that two variables are related but cannot establish which one is the cause and which is the effect.

questions.question: Half of participants receive condition A then B, and half receive B then A. What problem is this arrangement designed to reduce?
options: Coverage error in the sampling frame
questions.answer: Order and carryover effects
questions.explanation: Counterbalancing distributes practice, fatigue, and carryover effects across condition orders.

questions.question: For a study comparing two population means, the null hypothesis specifies that the population mean difference equals:
questions.answer: Zero
questions.explanation: For this specified comparison, the null hypothesis states no population mean difference; sample differences can still arise by chance.

questions.question: A researcher predicts that adding retrieval practice will increase the mean vocabulary score relative to ordinary review. Which statement is the hypothesis?
options: The score will be measured with a 20-item test
Retrieval practice will produce a higher mean score than ordinary review
questions.answer: Retrieval practice will produce a higher mean score than ordinary review
questions.explanation: The hypothesis is the testable predicted relationship between the manipulated study condition and the measured outcome.

questions.question: External validity is best improved by:
options: Using diverse samples and varied settings across studies
Increasing sample size of the original study
questions.answer: Using diverse samples and varied settings across studies
questions.explanation: External validity increases when findings hold across different participants, settings, and time periods.

questions.question: Two observers use the same behavior code but disagree often. Which improvement most directly targets inter-rater reliability?
options: Replace the target behavior with an unmeasured concept
Assign observers to different behaviors without a shared rule
Clarify the coding rule, train with examples, and check agreement on common intervals
questions.answer: Clarify the coding rule, train with examples, and check agreement on common intervals
questions.explanation: A precise codebook, shared practice, and agreement checks reduce inconsistent application of the same observational categories.

questions.question: The replication crisis refers to:
options: Many classic psychology findings failing to replicate
Studies being too expensive to repeat
Statistical methods being inconsistent across labs
questions.answer: Many classic psychology findings failing to replicate
questions.explanation: Large replication projects found that a substantial proportion of published psychology findings could not be reproduced.

questions.question: A study can cause mild distress but offers no plan for monitoring, stopping, or support. Which Belmont principle is most directly under-addressed?
questions.answer: Beneficence
questions.explanation: Beneficence requires minimizing foreseeable harm and using safeguards proportionate to risk.

questions.question: Publication bias leads to a scientific literature that:
options: Is perfectly representative of all research conducted
Favors qualitative studies over quantitative ones
questions.answer: Overrepresents statistically significant positive results
questions.explanation: Because positive findings are more likely to be published, the published literature overestimates effect sizes and the reliability of findings.

questions.question: Which design choice improves causal inference but does not by itself make a sample representative of the population?
questions.answer: Random assignment to experimental conditions
questions.explanation: Random assignment helps compare conditions by reducing systematic allocation bias; population representativeness depends on how the sample was selected.

questions.question: A study reports r = -0.72 between weekly stress score and sleep duration. What does the sign and magnitude indicate?
options: A proven causal effect of stress on sleep
A fairly strong negative association: higher stress tends to accompany less sleep
No relationship because the coefficient is negative
questions.answer: A fairly strong negative association: higher stress tends to accompany less sleep
questions.explanation: The negative sign indicates opposite movement and the magnitude indicates a relatively strong linear association; correlation alone does not establish causation.

questions.question: Ice-cream sales and sunburns rise together in summer. Which explanation best illustrates a third-variable account?
options: Hot, sunny weather increases both ice-cream buying and sun exposure
Sunburn must cause people to buy ice cream
Ice cream must chemically cause sunburn
questions.answer: Hot, sunny weather increases both ice-cream buying and sun exposure
questions.explanation: A shared cause can produce an association even when neither measured variable causes the other.

questions.question: A conceptual replication tests whether:
options: The original researchers' conclusions were accurate
The underlying theoretical claim holds using different methods or samples
Statistical analyses from the original study are correct
The original study's procedure can be run exactly as before
questions.answer: The underlying theoretical claim holds using different methods or samples
questions.explanation: Conceptual replications assess the generalizability of a theoretical finding using different operationalizations or populations.

questions.question: Which sampling method is most likely to produce a representative sample?
questions.answer: Simple random sampling
questions.explanation: Simple random sampling gives every population member an equal chance of selection, minimizing systematic bias.

questions.question: The WEIRD problem highlights that most psychology research over-represents:
options: Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic samples
questions.answer: Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic samples
questions.explanation: The WEIRD critique argues that generalizing from such samples to all of humanity is problematic given their unrepresentativeness.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? Internal validity is best ensured by:
options: A large number of survey questions only
Random assignment and experimental control of confounds
questions.answer: Random assignment and experimental control of confounds
questions.explanation: Internal validity is strengthened when alternative explanations are controlled, often through random assignment and careful design.

questions.question: A teacher informally labels students as “focused” without a stated rule. What change most directly improves measurement clarity?
options: Increase the number of treatment conditions
Define focus as a specified observable count or score
questions.answer: Define focus as a specified observable count or score
questions.explanation: An operational definition makes the construct measurable and allows the procedure to be applied consistently and evaluated for validity.

questions.question: A convenience sample is drawn only from an after-school club. What is the strongest immediate concern about generalizing to the whole school?
options: Coverage bias because many students had no chance to be sampled
questions.answer: Coverage bias because many students had no chance to be sampled
questions.explanation: A frame limited to club members systematically excludes other students, so the sample may not represent the target population.

questions.question: A low-risk study temporarily withholds its full purpose to prevent demand characteristics. Which safeguard is most directly required afterward?
options: Skipping consent because the risk was low
A prompt debriefing that explains the deception and gives an appropriate chance to withdraw data
Permanent concealment of the study purpose
questions.answer: A prompt debriefing that explains the deception and gives an appropriate chance to withdraw data
questions.explanation: When justified deception is used, debriefing restores information, explains the reason, addresses concerns, and protects participant autonomy.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? The goal of peer review is to:
options: Guarantee that every conclusion is correct
Evaluate a study's quality, logic, and evidence before publication
questions.answer: Evaluate a study's quality, logic, and evidence before publication
questions.explanation: Peer review is a quality-control process, though it does not guarantee that a study is flawless.

questions.question: A music condition is tested at 2 p.m. on tablets, while a quiet condition is tested at 8 a.m. on paper. Which redesign best supports a causal comparison?
options: Replace random assignment with volunteer choice
Keep both extra differences because they make groups distinct
Hold time and device constant so the intended sound condition is the main difference
Measure only the music group twice
questions.answer: Hold time and device constant so the intended sound condition is the main difference
questions.explanation: Standardizing time and device removes plausible alternative explanations for an outcome difference.

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate design to study changes in reading ability from ages 6 to 16?
questions.answer: Longitudinal study
questions.explanation: A longitudinal study follows the same individuals over time, directly tracking developmental changes in reading ability.

questions.question: In Experimental Psychology final concepts, A p-value represents:
options: The probability of observing results at least as extreme as found, assuming the null is true
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The effect size of the study
questions.answer: The probability of observing results at least as extreme as found, assuming the null is true
questions.explanation: The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, calculated under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true.
